forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

summary.summary: A pre-audit covering report asking the committee to approve Wyre's 2025/26 Statement of Accounts; the draft was certified by the s151 officer and published by the 30 June 2026 statutory deadline. The report itself carries no figures — the accounts, capital financing report, revenue variances and the reserves and balances statements all sit in appendices published separately, with the outturn to be folded into the Medium Term Financial Plan 2026/27 to 2030/31. The substantive disclosure is on audit: Wyre's 2024/25 accounts were signed off in February 2026 under the national 'backstop' arrangements with a disclaimed opinion (the auditor gave no assurance on the numbers), and the council says it will be subject to disclaimed opinions for at least another year, with 2025/26 post-audit sign-off expected at or soon after the November 2026 committee.

signals.why: Until a real audit opinion returns, lenders have no external assurance over Wyre's reported balances — a sector-wide backstop condition, but one the council itself confirms will persist.

signals.headline: Draft 2025/26 Statement of Accounts certified and published by the 30 June 2026 statutory deadline; formal approval due by 31 January 2027

news_drafts.headline: Wyre says new borrowing is not affordable while it projects a £4m gap in 2030/31
news_drafts.lead:
Wyre Council's finance director has told members that new borrowing is "not considered to be affordable, prudent or sustainable" while the council projects a £4m gap between spending and income in 2030/31. The statement is in the treasury management questions and answers paper prepared for the Overview and Scrutiny Committee, which met on 16 November 2026.

The paper sets out an illustrative case. A £2m loan taken in February 2027 from the Public Works Loan Board, the government's lending arm for councils and the source of most council borrowing, would carry a projected rate of 6.40%. Principal and interest would come to approximately £208,000 a year over 25 years. The paper gives the figure in the context of capital works the council is assessing.

The papers do not say which capital works are under assessment, or whether any borrowing is planned for them.

news_drafts.headline: Wyre auditor KPMG expected to disclaim opinion on 2025/26 accounts but finds no significant value-for-money risks
news_drafts.lead:
Wyre Council's external auditor, KPMG, is expected to disclaim its opinion on the council's 2025/26 accounts, as it did for 2024/25, the Audit and Standards Committee was told. A disclaimed opinion means the auditor has not been able to give a view on the accounts. The minutes say this reflects "the legacy of previous audits completed by Deloitte". The government's "building back assurance process" is designed to help councils obtain clean opinions before Local Government Reorganisation (LGR), the merger of councils into new unitary authorities.

Separately, KPMG's value for money assessment, the auditor's view of whether the council manages its money and decisions properly, found no significant risks. It covered financial sustainability, governance, and improving efficiency and effectiveness. The minutes record that "no significant risks had been identified within the assessment undertaken". KPMG's full value for money conclusion will come to the committee's November meeting.

The committee also heard about costs at Marine Hall, the council's entertainment venue, which recorded an operating deficit of £718,000 in 2025/26. Around £200,000 of that came from premises costs, with just under £67,000 from electricity. Officers said additional investment is planned for the theatre, which would then pass to the new unitary authority after LGR. The minutes give no timescale or cost for that work.

Members were also told that spending on water rose by £66,000 during the year. The Finance Team is investigating the increase, and its findings have not yet been reported to the committee. The council also provided £284,000 to Lancaster University for work on Our Future Coast, Wyre's coastal defence scheme.

findings.headline: Prior-year value for money recommendation on budget holder involvement in budget setting is reported as implemented in 2025/26
findings.detail: The council's response to the earlier observation says finance officers and budget managers work together on budget development and that a sign-off proforma will be used for the 2026/27 budget. The update status is recorded as implemented in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Budget ownership by service managers is a control finance directors at other councils often struggle to evidence, so a documented sign-off process is a concrete reference point.

findings.headline: Scale fee for the 2025/26 audit is set at £161,561 plus VAT, against £157,161 in 2024/25, with a fee variation under consideration
findings.detail: KPMG says it is considering the impact of the land and buildings valuation problems on its audit fees, and is working with management ahead of the 2026/27 audit to address the valuation issues.
findings.matters: Additional fees from audit delay or valuation problems are a cost a finance director at another council would want to anticipate when reviewing audit contracts.
findings.figures: £161,561 plus VAT scale fee for 2025/26; £157,161 scale fee for 2024/25
findings.quote: Our scale fee for the 2025/26 audit, as set by PSAA is £161,561 plus VAT (£157,161 in 2024/25).

findings.headline: Auditor has identified no risks of a significant weakness in the council's value for money arrangements, with no significant weaknesses found in financial sustainability, governance, or economy, efficiency and effectiveness
findings.detail: KPMG's value for money commentary covers all three domains and records no significant weaknesses. It raises one performance improvement observation, on Cabinet review of the strategic risk register.
findings.matters: Clean value for money conclusions alongside a disclaimed accounts opinion show the council's arrangements are assessed separately from the accounts problems, which peers and lenders would read differently.
findings.quote: As noted on the right, we have identified no risks of a significant weakness in the Council’s arrangements to secure value for money.

findings.headline: Auditor reports that the risk on the post retirement benefit obligation valuation has decreased, with no material misstatement found in the LGPS figures of £93.5m liabilities and £128.9m assets
findings.detail: The auditor found the actuary independent and of appropriate expertise, and agreed the actuarial results and accounting treatment were reasonable. It noted that management assumptions were optimistic for CPI, though still within the auditor's reasonable range.
findings.matters: A pension valuation that passes audit with no material misstatement is a reference point for other councils with LGPS deficits or surpluses, which the paper notes are becoming more common.
findings.figures: £93.5m present value of defined benefit obligations; £128.9m fair value of plan assets; £37.0m asset ceiling impact
findings.quote: We completed our planned procedures, and we did not identify any material misstatements relating to this area.

findings.headline: Uncorrected audit misstatements of £582k are recorded against income, surplus for the year and total assets
findings.detail: The uncorrected misstatements table shows a £582k item against income, with the same £582k shown against surplus for the year and total assets. The table gives percentages alongside each line.
findings.matters: Uncorrected misstatements that flow through income and the surplus show the size of unresolved adjustments that finance teams would need to understand before accepting the reported result.
findings.figures: £582k income; £582k surplus for the year (shown as a reduction); £582k total assets (shown as a reduction); 0.84%; 3.3%; 0.23%
